title: The Tannisho, part one
hookLine: read Shinran's sayings as remembered by his student
tomorrow: the student who wrote it all down was worried. about what?

cards: Some creators call their followers a family; some coaches post about their students like trophies. Shinran, the Japanese Pure Land teacher, had people walking long roads to hear him.

And in the Tannisho, the short record of his sayings kept by his student Yuien, Shinran says, in paraphrase: I don't have even one disciple. Not one. Coming from a teacher with followers, that sounds like false modesty.

teach.b: Here's his reason, in paraphrase. If I brought people to say the nembutsu, the name of Amida Buddha, by my own effort, they'd be my disciples. But they say it because Amida's working moves them.
So how could I call them mine?

teach.h: TARIKI: THE VOW DOES THE WORK.
teach.b: That's other power, tariki: the trust and the practice come from Amida's vow, not from the teacher's skill or the student's. The same record opens on this note.
When the thought of saying the nembutsu arises, Yuien remembers Shinran saying, a person is already embraced, never to be abandoned, and the vow doesn't sort people by young or old, good or bad.

Then, a line that widens the circle: Shinran says he never once said the nembutsu for his own parents alone, because every living being has been his father and mother, brother and sister, through countless lives.
Everyone is family. A neighbor tradition knows the shape of this.

teach.h: PAUL: GRACE, THE GIFT OF GOD.
teach.b: In the King James Version, Paul writes: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” Shared: something given, not earned, and no room to boast. And an honest difference.

For Paul, grace is the gift of God, the creator, through Christ. For Shinran, the gift is the vow of Amida, a Buddha, and Shin Buddhists don't speak of Amida as the maker of the world. Close cousins, and not the same.
Other power, either way, is the end of keeping score.

how: In Jodo Shinshu (Shin Buddhism), members say the nembutsu, Namu Amida Butsu, as an expression of gratitude rather than a technique, and the Tannisho is widely read in study groups.

s: Shinran said he had many disciples and was proud of them
the record has him say he has not even one: people say the nembutsu by Amida's working, not his.
in the Tannisho, the vow doesn't sort people by young or old, good or bad
Yuien remembers this near the record's opening.
Shinran's other power and Paul's grace are exactly the same teaching
both speak of a gift not earned; for Paul it's God's grace through Christ, for Shinran Amida Buddha's vow.

games.q: a coach who built a winning team says in a speech, 'these aren't my players; the game made them.' what would Shinran recognize?
o: not claiming people as his own, since something beyond him did the work.
false modesty; a good coach should take the credit that's earned.
a sign the coach didn't really try; real teachers shape students.
games.why: Shinran refused to call anyone his disciple because the saying of the name came from Amida's working, not from him.

practice: Count, slowly, things in your life you didn't earn: the language you speak, someone who taught you to read, a meal someone else cooked, the breath arriving right now. One finger for each.
When the count runs out, keep breathing, and notice that the breath isn't something you're making happen, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Tannisho: a short record of Shinran's sayings, written down by his student Yuien. In its first part, the teacher won't call anyone his own.

orig.note: Japanese: other (他) power (力), the power of Amida's vow, as opposed to jiriki, self power.
